title: Consistent Hashing: distribute data across nodes so adding/removing a node moves only K/N keys (not all), used in distributed caches and databases.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a ring and assigns each key to the first node clockwise from it.
Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of the keys, not nearly all as naive modulo hashing would.
Virtual nodes give each physical node many ring positions, smoothing out uneven key distribution and load.
It is the backbone of distributed caches (Memcached), databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB), and partitioned systems.
Replication is achieved by walking clockwise to the next N distinct physical nodes from the key's position.
Weighting virtual node counts lets heterogeneous hardware carry proportional load.
The problem it solves is the instability of modulo hashing, where changing the node count reshuffles nearly every key.

s1_definition.oneliner: Place nodes and keys on a hash ring and assign each key to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only a small slice of keys, not all of them.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Consistent hashing** : a distribution technique that maps both data keys and server nodes onto a conceptual ring using a hash function.
- **Key assignment** : each key belongs to the first node encountered clockwise from the key's hash position on the ring.
- **Minimal movement** : adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of the keys, instead of nearly all as modulo hashing would.
- **Virtual nodes** : each physical node is placed at many points on the ring to smooth out distribution and balance load.
- **Replication** : achieved by walking clockwise to the next N distinct physical nodes, placing copies on different machines.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India stores customer records across several branches by taking the account number modulo the branch count. If one branch opens or closes, the count changes, and suddenly almost every customer's record maps to a different branch, forcing a massive migration. Consistent hashing is a smarter scheme: picture a clock face with branches placed around it, and each customer placed on the clock too, assigned to the next branch clockwise. If one branch closes, only the customers between it and the previous branch move; everyone else stays put.

```text
                   Consistent Hashing Ring

                        0 / 2^32
                          │
                    ┌─────┴─────┐
                    │           │
               Node A         Node B
              (vnode x3)     (vnode x3)
                    │           │
        key1 ───►  │           │ ◄─── key3
                    │           │
                    │   Node C  │
                    │  (vnode x3)│
                    │     │     │
            key2 ───┘     │     └─── key4
                          │
                     wraps around

  Adding Node D:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Before: A owns arc [C..A], B owns [A..B]    │
  │ After:  D inserted between A and B          │
  │         D takes keys in [A..D] from B       │
  │         A, C: unchanged                     │
  │         Only ~1/4 of keys move              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Virtual nodes: each physical node has many ring points
  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐
  │A1│ │B1│ │C1│ │A2│ │B2│ │C2│ │A3│ │B3│ │C3│
  └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘
  Fine interleaving = even load distribution
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Consistent hashing is a distribution technique that maps both data keys and server nodes onto a conceptual ring and assigns each key to the first node clockwise from it. Its defining property is that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys, instead of nearly all as naive modulo hashing would. That minimal-movement property is what makes it the backbone of distributed caches and databases.

The problem it solves is the instability of modulo hashing. If I place a key on node = hash(key) % nodeCount, then changing the node count changes the result for almost every key. In a distributed cache that means a near-total cache-miss storm every time I scale. At National Bank of India, exactly this happened: we cached balances with account number modulo node count, and adding a node during growth remapped nearly every balance, emptied the cache, and triggered a storm of database reads.

Consistent hashing fixes this by hashing each node to one or more points on a ring and each key to a point, with a key owned by the first node clockwise from it. When I add a node, it takes over only the keys in the arcs between it and its predecessors. The practical refinement is virtual nodes: placing each physical node at many points finely interleaves the arcs and balances load, and weighting the number of virtual points lets stronger hardware carry proportionally more.

Consistent hashing also enables replication by walking clockwise to the next N distinct nodes, which is exactly how Cassandra and DynamoDB place replicas. That combination of minimal key movement, virtual-node balancing, and clockwise replication is why consistent hashing is the standard way to distribute data across a changing set of nodes.

Remember one sentence: consistent hashing places keys and nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only 1/N of the keys, not nearly all.
